PAPER 1 — DRAFT

Working title: Who is left behind? Spatial equity and public perception of public EV charging infrastructure in a developing-country megaregion — evidence from West Java, Indonesia

Target journal (primary): Energy Research & Social Science (Elsevier, Q1) Alternatives: Energy Policy (Q1) · Journal of Transport Geography (Q1)

Draft note: numbers below are drawn from the project datasets (PLN UID West Java Master SPKLU & transaction detail, March 2026; ABSA public-review corpus; BPS socio-economic indicators). Verify every figure against the source tables before submission. Citations marked [VERIFY] are placeholders for real references you must insert.

Structured abstract (≈250 words)

Context. Indonesia is scaling public EV charging (SPKLU) rapidly under its 2030 electric-mobility targets, but whether this build-out is equitable — and whether users perceive it as reliable and accessible — remains unmeasured at sub-national scale.

Objective. We evaluate the distributive equity and public perception of the public SPKLU network in West Java, Indonesia's most populous province, and test whether equity and perceived service quality are linked.

Data & methods. We integrate (i) the official Master SPKLU registry (636 charging units across 348 sites in 26 cities/regencies), (ii) 101,020 real charging transactions (≈2.26 GWh, March 2026), (iii) a corpus of 894 user-reviewed locations (584 quantitatively scored on a Service Quality Index, SQI), and (iv) BPS population, HDI and income-tier indicators. We compute Gini coefficients and Lorenz curves for unit and consumption distribution, normalise them by population and income, construct an Equity Priority Index (EPI = underserved × low-income), and contrast urban (cities) versus rural (regencies) provision. We then model the drivers of perceived service quality from review aspect-sentiment.

Results. Provision is moderately-to-highly unequal: the unit-vs-population Gini is ≈0.19 while the consumption-vs-population Gini reaches ≈0.45, indicating demand (and effective access) concentrates far more than the hardware itself. Cities dominate both coverage and intensity; several low-income regencies are simultaneously under-served and high-need (high EPI). Public perception is driven primarily by reliability and availability, not by amenities — and the lowest-SQI locations cluster in the same under-served peripheries, suggesting equity and experienced quality reinforce one another.

Implications. A coverage-first roll-out can mask a reliability and distributive gap. We translate the findings into a transferable, equity-weighted prioritisation framework for just EV-charging deployment in emerging economies.

Keywords: EV charging; energy justice; spatial equity; public perception; Gini/Lorenz; Indonesia; just transition

1. Introduction

  • The global EV transition and the role of public fast charging in countries with low private-charging access (apartments, kampung housing) — charging equity matters more where home charging is rare. [VERIFY]
  • Gap 1: most charging-equity work is on high-income contexts (US/EU/China); Southeast Asia and developing megaregions are under-studied. [VERIFY]
  • Gap 2: equity studies rarely link distributive metrics to perceived/experienced service quality from real users.
  • Setting: West Java (≈50M people, Indonesia's largest province), PLN's RACE-for-2030 electrification push.
  • Contribution: (1) first integrated distributive-equity + perception assessment of SPKLU at provincial scale on real operational data; (2) an Equity Priority Index combining under-service and socio-economic need; (3) evidence that distributive and experiential gaps coincide.
  • Research questions:
  • RQ1 (Distributive equity): How unequally are charging units and consumption distributed across West Java, and does normalising by population/income change the picture?
  • RQ2 (Urban–rural): How large is the urban (city) vs rural (regency) disparity in coverage and usage intensity?
  • RQ3 (Perception): Which service aspects most determine perceived charging quality (SQI)?
  • RQ4 (Linkage): Do under-served, low-income areas also experience lower perceived quality — i.e., does inequity compound?

2. Literature & framing

  • Energy-justice triad (distributive, procedural, recognition) as the organising lens. [VERIFY: Sovacool & Dworkin; Jenkins et al.]
  • Charging-equity / accessibility literature and methods (Gini/Lorenz, 2SFCA, EPI-type indices). [VERIFY: Hsu & Fingerman; Khan et al.; Carlton & Sultana]
  • Perception / service-quality of charging (reliability, uptime, availability). [VERIFY]
  • Position the paper: distributive + experiential, developing-country, operational data.

3. Study area, data & methods

3.1 Study area

West Java: 26 cities/regencies; urban cores (e.g., Bekasi, Bogor, Depok, Bandung) vs rural regencies; demographic & income heterogeneity (Klassen typology 2023).

3.2 Data

SourceContentScope
Master SPKLU (PLN)636 units · 348 sites · coordinates · operator (PLN/partner)26 kota/kab
Transaction detail101,020 sessions · 2.26 GWh · kWh, duration, tariff, AC/DCMarch 2026 (330 active stations)
ABSA review corpusaspect-level sentiment; SQI894 locations (584 scored)
BPS / Klassenpopulation (SP2022), HDI, poverty, income tierper kota/kab

3.3 Methods

  • Distributive equity: Lorenz curves & Gini for (a) units vs population, (b) consumption (kWh) vs population; interpret the gap between them.
  • Normalisation: units-per-100k, kWh-per-capita, EV-per-100k.
  • Equity Priority Index: EPI = standardised(under-service) × standardised(low-income), to flag high-need under-served areas.
  • Urban–rural: city vs regency contrasts on coverage and kWh/unit (utilisation/pressure proxy).
  • Perception model: dependent var = SQI; predictors = aspect sentiments (reliability, availability, facilities, location, price…); feature-importance / regression on 584 scored locations.
  • Linkage (RQ4): spatial correlation between EPI / under-service and mean SQI.
  • Robustness: sensitivity of Gini to active-vs-all stations; note Gini is an equity proxy pending fuller socio-spatial controls.

4. Results

  • R1 — Distribution (RQ1): unit-vs-pop Gini ≈ 0.19; consumption-vs-pop Gini ≈ 0.45. Lorenz curves show hardware is moderately concentrated but use is far more concentrated → effective access gap. (Fig. 1 Lorenz; Table 1 per-kota.)
  • R2 — Urban–rural (RQ2): cities hold the bulk of units and far higher kWh/unit; regencies show coverage thin-ness and, where present, high utilisation pressure. (Fig. 2.)
  • R3 — Equity Priority (RQ1/RQ2): identify the high-EPI under-served, low-income regencies (name them from the EPI table). (Fig. 3 EPI map.)
  • R4 — Perception drivers (RQ3): reliability and availability dominate SQI; facilities/price secondary. (Fig. 4 driver importance; mean SQI ≈ [insert mean_jabar].)
  • R5 — Compounding (RQ4): under-served / high-EPI areas also show lower mean SQI → distributive and experiential disadvantage coincide. (Fig. 5 EPI vs SQI scatter.)

5. Discussion

  • Coverage-first metrics flatter the network; a reliability-and-distribution lens reveals the real gap (link to the national finding that ~a third of stations sit "offline" — see Paper 2).
  • Energy-justice reading: distributive shortfall + recognition gap (peripheral, lower-income communities) + procedural (deployment logic favours demand-dense cities).
  • Policy: equity-weighted siting, uptime/SLA mandates, targeted support for high-EPI regencies; pairing new builds with reliability guarantees.
  • Generalisability to other emerging megaregions (low home-charging access → public-charging equity is decisive).

6. Limitations

  • Single-month transaction window; Gini as equity proxy; perception from a review corpus (self-selection); SQI construct validity; no individual-level access modelling (future: isochrone/2SFCA accessibility).

7. Conclusion

Distributive and experienced inequities in West Java's SPKLU network are real and mutually reinforcing; an equity-weighted, reliability-aware deployment framework is needed for a just EV transition in developing economies.

Figures/Tables plan

  1. Lorenz curves (units & kWh vs population) + Gini. 2. Urban–rural coverage & kWh/unit. 3. EPI choropleth. 4. SQI driver importance. 5. EPI vs SQI scatter. T1: per-kota integrated table. T2: perception aspect summary.

Data & ethics

Data-availability statement; PLN data-use permission; review-corpus collection ethics & ToS compliance; de-identification.

Suggested literature to position against (VERIFY exact citations)

Energy-justice frameworks; EV charging accessibility/equity (US/EU/China); 2SFCA & Gini in infrastructure equity; charging reliability/uptime studies; Indonesia EV-policy papers.

PAPER 2 — DRAFT

Working title: From coverage to capability: data-driven siting and a utilisation–availability diagnosis of a rapidly scaling national EV-charging network — a transaction-level study of Indonesia

Target journal (primary): Sustainable Cities and Society (Elsevier, Q1) Alternatives: Applied Energy (Q1) · eTransportation (Q1) · Computers, Environment and Urban Systems (Q1, if the GIS/MCDA method is the headline)

Draft note: figures are from the project datasets (national Master SPKLU registry & monthly consumption series 2024–2026; West Java transaction detail, March 2026; Jakarta Raya + West Java transaction detail, 1–8 June 2026). Province assignment for national points is estimated from coordinates — state this explicitly. Verify all numbers; [VERIFY] marks placeholder citations.

Structured abstract (≈250 words)

Context. EV-charging research overwhelmingly measures coverage — how many chargers, and where. Far less is known about whether a fast-growing national network is capable: actually available, well-utilised, and sited where demand is.

Objective. Using one of the largest operational EV-charging datasets reported for a developing country, we (i) characterise the explosive growth and spatial structure of Indonesia's public SPKLU network, (ii) diagnose an under-examined availability gap, (iii) quantify which kinds of locations actually sell energy, and (iv) propose and validate a transferable, transaction-grounded site-selection and commercial-viability framework.

Data & methods. We combine the national Master SPKLU registry (≈3,200 sites; location, capacity, operator, operational status), the national monthly consumption series (Jan 2024–Jun 2026), and transaction-level detail for West Java (101,020 sessions, Mar 2026) and Jakarta Raya (56,740 sessions over 8 days, Jun 2026). Methods: growth and concentration analysis; an operational-status diagnosis; a venue-type ("sector") utilisation classifier; and a multi-criteria (MCDA) weighted-overlay siting model extended with catchment, competitor/cannibalisation and a simple payback model, validated against observed per-venue utilisation.

Results. National energy sold rose ≈5× in one year (≈9.1→48.6 GWh, 2024→2025) with a 2026 run-rate near 10 GWh/month; demand is heavily Java-centric (~67% of sites). Crucially, ~32% of stations report an "offline" operational state — a reliability gap invisible to coverage maps. Utilisation is highly venue-dependent: toll-road rest areas sell ~3.5× the energy per site of a utility-office charger and ~13× a hotel charger; midday-peaking, DC-dominated demand in Jakarta indicates a commercial/fleet usage rhythm. Our siting model reproduces these patterns and ranks candidate sites by payback.

Implications. "More chargers" is the wrong objective; capable chargers — available, high-throughput, demand-matched — is the right one. We offer an open, reproducible siting toolkit for emerging-economy charging networks.

Keywords: EV charging; site selection; MCDA; utilisation; availability/reliability; smart cities; Indonesia

1. Introduction

  • Charging networks in emerging economies are scaling faster than they are being evaluated; coverage metrics dominate, capability metrics (availability, utilisation, demand-match) are neglected. [VERIFY]
  • Three blind spots: (a) availability/uptime rarely measured at network scale; (b) utilisation by location type rarely quantified on real energy data; (c) site-selection methods rarely validated against observed demand.
  • Contributions: (1) a national growth + spatial + availability diagnosis on operational data; (2) a venue-type utilisation taxonomy (where charging actually "sells"); (3) a transaction-validated MCDA + commercial-viability siting framework with catchment & cannibalisation; (4) an open, reproducible dashboard implementation.
  • Research questions:
  • RQ1 (Growth & structure): How fast, and how spatially concentrated, is the network's demand?
  • RQ2 (Availability): What share of stations are non-operational, and where?
  • RQ3 (Utilisation by venue): Which location types deliver the most energy per site, and why?
  • RQ4 (Siting): Can an MCDA + catchment + payback model reproduce observed utilisation and rank new sites credibly?

2. Related work

  • EV charging demand & utilisation modelling. [VERIFY]
  • Charging-station site selection (MCDA/AHP/GIS, optimisation). [VERIFY: reviews of EVCS siting]
  • Reliability/uptime of public charging (mostly high-income contexts). [VERIFY]
  • Gap statement: combine all three on a national, developing-country, transaction-level dataset.

3. Data & methods

3.1 Data

SourceContentScope
National Master SPKLU~3,200 sites: coords, capacity, status, charger/connector count, PLN/non-PLNIndonesia (province estimated from coordinates)
National consumption seriesmonthly sessions, kWh, revenueJan 2024 – Jun 2026
West Java transactions101,020 sessions, 2.26 GWh, AC/DC, durationMar 2026
Jakarta Raya transactions56,740 sessions, 1.29 GWh, hourly/UP3/kota/power1–8 Jun 2026

3.2 Methods

  • Growth & concentration (RQ1): monthly series; year-on-year multiples; island/province share (note coordinate-based province estimation + Jakarta bounding-box correction).
  • Availability diagnosis (RQ2): classify operational status (available / in-use / offline / unavailable / maintenance); map and quantify the offline share by region; discuss measurement caveats (snapshot vs sustained downtime).
  • Venue utilisation (RQ3): keyword classifier assigns each station to a venue sector (toll rest area, mall, hotel, dealer, PLN office, F&B, hospital, public/transport, residential, etc.); compare kWh per site, sessions/site, kWh/session, mean power, dwell; interpret via dwell-time × charger-power × captive-demand mechanism. (West Java has per-site energy; national has site counts.)
  • Siting model (RQ4): min–max-normalised MCDA weighted overlay (demand, growth, supply-gap, equity) at area level; point-level candidate scoring by distance-to-nearest-SPKLU + host demand; catchment (radius/iso-proxy), competitor/cannibalisation scan (PLN vs private), and a commercial-viability score + simple payback anchored to observed sessions/unit/month. Validate by checking the model ranks high-utilisation venue types (toll/dealer) above low ones (hotel).

4. Results

  • R1 — Hockey-stick growth (RQ1): ≈9.1 GWh (2024) → ≈48.6 GWh (2025), ~5.3×; 2026 run-rate ~10 GWh/month (~120 GWh/yr trajectory); ~2.4M registered users. Java ≈67% of sites; private sector ≈32% of the network. (Fig. 1 growth; Fig. 2 island/province shares.)
  • R2 — Availability gap (RQ2): ~32% of stations in "offline" state (≈1,000 of ~3,200); available ≈49%, in-use ≈16%. Map the offline share by region. Headline: coverage maps overstate effective capacity. (Fig. 3 condition map; Table 1 status by region.)
  • R3 — Where charging sells (RQ3): ranked kWh/site (West Java, Mar 2026): toll rest area ≈18,700, auto dealer ≈17,300, mall ≈10,100, …, PLN office ≈5,400, hotel ≈1,400. → toll ≈3.5× a utility office, ≈13× a hotel. Mechanism: captive transit demand + high DC power + short dwell = high turnover; amenity AC sites idle. Jakarta June: DC-dominant, midday-peaking (fleet/ride-hail rhythm), demand concentrated in South/East Jakarta. (Fig. 4 venue ranking; Fig. 5 power-vs-intensity; Fig. 6 Jakarta hourly.)
  • R4 — Siting validation (RQ4): the MCDA + catchment + payback model ranks transit/dealer venues highest and saturated/amenity sites lowest, consistent with observed utilisation; example candidate rankings + payback ranges. (Fig. 7 candidate map; Table 2 viability/payback.)

5. Discussion

  • Reframe the policy objective from coverage → capability (available + utilised + demand-matched).
  • Availability as the cheapest capacity: fixing offline stations may add more effective charging than new builds.
  • Demand-matched siting: bias toward transit corridors / high-throughput DC; treat hotels/offices as amenity, not revenue.
  • Grid as the missing layer (distance to substation/feeder, spare transformer capacity) — the operator's informational advantage; flag as future integration.
  • Transferability to other emerging-economy networks.

6. Limitations

  • Province assignment estimated from coordinates (nearest-centroid + Jakarta bbox) — aggregate-robust, not site-exact.
  • National per-station transactions unavailable (status counters reset to ~0) → utilisation depth shown for West Java + Jakarta only; national consumption is a country total (not region-split).
  • "Offline" is a snapshot status (may over/understate sustained downtime).
  • Venue classifier is heuristic (a small share mis-bucketed); payback model is indicative, not a financial quotation.

7. Conclusion

A rapidly scaling network can be wide yet not deep: Indonesia's SPKLU footprint is impressive, but ~a third sits offline and utilisation is sharply venue-dependent. A capability-first, demand-matched, reliability-aware deployment strategy — embodied in our open siting toolkit — better serves the EV transition than coverage alone.

Figures/Tables plan

  1. National monthly growth. 2. Island/province shares. 3. National condition map (status-coloured). 4. kWh/site by venue. 5. Power-vs-intensity quadrant. 6. Jakarta hourly rhythm. 7. Candidate-siting map + payback. T1: status by region. T2: candidate viability/payback. T3: venue utilisation summary.

Reproducibility & data

Open dashboard implementation; aggregation scripts; data-availability statement; province-estimation method disclosed; PLN data-use permission.

Suggested literature to position against (VERIFY exact citations)

EVCS site-selection reviews (MCDA/AHP/GIS/optimisation); charging utilisation & demand studies; public-charging reliability/uptime; smart-city infrastructure analytics; Indonesia/SE-Asia EV transition.

papers.html:
Comparative Analysis of Electric Vehicle Markets, Charging Tariffs, and Charge-Point-Operator Business Models in ASEAN: Market Structures, Investment Attractiveness, and Indonesia’s Position (2025–2026)

Qashtalani Haramaini

Department of Urban Planning and Design / RACE for 2030 Program, Monash University Indonesia; Department of Electrical Engineering, Universitas Indonesia

Working paper — September 2026

Abstract

The ten ASEAN economies are frequently analysed as a single electric vehicle (EV) market, yet their charging-infrastructure businesses operate under structurally incompatible rules. This paper compares EV adoption, retail charging tariffs, charge-point-operator (CPO) economics, and market/regulatory structures across the six major ASEAN markets — Indonesia, Thailand, Vietnam, Malaysia, Singapore, and the Philippines — using 2025–2026 data drawn from regulators, utilities, operator rate cards, and reputable secondary research. We document a five-fold spread in retail DC fast-charging prices (from ≈US$0.15/kWh in Vietnam’s captive V-Green network and Indonesia’s regulated SPKLU tariff to ≈US$0.70/kWh in Singapore) and classify national market structures into five archetypes: captive vertical integration (Vietnam), open multi-CPO competition (Thailand), utility-anchored partnership (Indonesia), licensed-tender regulation (Singapore), and government-linked-company-led deployment (Malaysia), with a mandate-driven early market in the Philippines. No leadership verdict holds across all investment segments: Thailand leads vehicle manufacturing, Indonesia leads battery/upstream integration, Vietnam leads volume adoption and build-out speed, and Singapore leads per-station profitability. Indonesia holds the region’s largest deployment pipeline (4,655 public SPKLU units in 2025 against a 31,859-unit 2030 target) and doubled BEV sales, home-charging subscriptions, and public-charger growth in a single year, but capped per-session service fees, low utilization outside Java, and an archipelagic geography compress private CPO unit economics. We conclude with segment-specific investment guidance and policy options — including utilization-linked incentives and cross-subsidy mechanisms — that would reconcile Indonesia’s efficiency–spatial-equity trade-off in charger deployment.

Keywords: electric vehicles; charging infrastructure; SPKLU; charge point operator; ASEAN; tariff regulation; market structure; Indonesia

1. Introduction

Southeast Asia has become one of the fastest-scaling EV regions in the world. Battery-electric vehicles (BEVs) reached 21% of new passenger-car sales across the six major ASEAN economies in the first half of 2026, up from 12% a year earlier [1], and Ember reports that ASEAN adoption levels in Singapore, Vietnam, Thailand, and Indonesia now exceed those of legacy automotive markets including the United States and the European Union [2]. Regional vehicle-market data likewise show EV sales growing 74.3% year-on-year in H1 2026, led by Vietnam (48.4% of regional EV volume) and Indonesia (22.2%) [3].

Behind this aggregate boom, however, the region is not one market. The commercial logic of building and operating charging infrastructure — who may sell electricity to vehicles, at what price, under which licence, and with what returns — differs so sharply between neighbouring countries that investment strategies transfer poorly across borders. A charge-point operator (CPO) model that is profitable in Bangkok may be legally impossible in Hanoi and financially unattractive in Surabaya.

This paper makes three contributions. First, it assembles a verifiable, source-dated comparison of retail charging tariffs, adoption figures, infrastructure counts, and CPO economics across the six major ASEAN markets for 2025–2026. Second, it proposes a five-archetype typology of ASEAN charging-market structures and uses it to explain observed price and deployment differences from first principles. Third, it locates Indonesia within this landscape and derives implications for investors and for Indonesian policy, with particular attention to the tension between deployment efficiency and spatial equity that arises under Indonesia’s regulated-tariff, utility-anchored model.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 describes data and methodology. Section 3 presents comparative results across adoption, pricing, market structure, infrastructure, and business economics. Section 4 discusses market leadership by investment segment and analyses Indonesia’s position. Section 5 draws policy and investment implications, and Section 6 concludes.

2. Data and Methodology

The study is a comparative desk-research analysis covering Indonesia, Thailand, Vietnam, Malaysia, Singapore, and the Philippines, with Brunei, Cambodia, Laos, and Myanmar excluded from quantitative comparison due to the absence of reliable data (an acknowledged gap; these four markets remain at very early stages of adoption). Data were collected between mid-2025 and September 2026 and prioritized in the following order: (i) primary regulatory and utility sources — Kementerian ESDM and PT PLN (Persero) for Indonesia [4–6], Thailand’s Board of Investment and Department of Energy Business [20, 22], Singapore’s Ministry of Transport and LTA [11, 12], Malaysia’s MEVnet census [14], and the Philippine Department of Energy accreditation framework [16]; (ii) operator-published rate cards (V-Green, PEA Volta, EA Anywhere, EV Station PluZ, Gentari, JomCharge, SP Mobility, Shell Recharge) [7, 10, 11, 13]; and (iii) reputable secondary research (Maybank Research, Ember, ICCT, Nikkei/KrASIA, USGS) [1, 2, 24, 25, 31].

Three methodological cautions govern the comparisons. First, currency conversion uses indicative mid-2026 rates (USD 1 ≈ IDR 16,300; THB 33; VND 26,000; MYR 4.2; SGD 1.28; PHP 57); converted figures are approximations. Second, charger counts are not unit-comparable across countries: Indonesia reports SPKLU machines, Singapore reports charging points, and Vietnam’s V-Green reports “ports” that include two-wheeler outlets and partly planned capacity; we therefore avoid cross-country charger-density league tables and flag definitional differences wherever counts are juxtaposed. Third, where sources conflict — notably ASEAN market-size projections (Mordor Intelligence US$5.99 billion for 2026 [27] versus MarkWide Research US$18.7 billion [28]) and Indonesian 2025 sales totals (Gaikindo/Just Auto 106,644 BEV units [23] versus Focus2move 99,755 [3]) — both figures are reported and treated as vendor estimates rather than settled facts.

3. Results

3.1 Adoption: a three-tier region

Figure 1 summarizes BEV penetration of new passenger-car sales in H1 2026. The region divides into three tiers: a high-adoption tier (Singapore ≈62%, Vietnam ≈35%), a mid tier (Thailand and Indonesia, each reported in a 22–30% band), and an early tier (Philippines ≈10%, Malaysia ≈6%) [1]. Outside Vietnam — whose transition is driven by the domestic champion VinFast, which sold 175,099 EVs domestically in 2025 — Chinese manufacturers account for an estimated 80–90% of ASEAN EV sales [1]. In Indonesia, BYD-group brands alone captured 51% of the 106,644 BEV units wholesaled in 2025 [23].

3.2 Charging tariffs: a five-fold price spread

Retail DC fast-charging prices span roughly a factor of five across the region (Figure 2, Table 1). Vietnam’s V-Green charges a flat 3,858 VND/kWh (≈US$0.148, VAT-inclusive) — but exclusively to VinFast vehicles [7]. Indonesia’s regulated SPKLU tariff is comparably low on the energy component (Rp2,466–2,475/kWh ≈ US$0.15) but adds a per-session service fee capped by ministerial decree at Rp25,000 for fast charging and Rp57,000 for ultra-fast charging, exclusive of VAT [4, 5]. Thailand’s open multi-CPO market prices between 5.30 and 9.50 THB/kWh with time-of-use differentiation [10]; Malaysia’s unregulated market spans RM0.85–1.80/kWh with location-based pricing and annual subscription discounts [13]; Philippine operators charge ₱20–38/kWh [17]; and Singapore’s licensed operators command S$0.55–0.89/kWh — the region’s highest — supported by high utilization and willingness to pay [11].

The structural insight is that price levels track market structure more than cost: the two cheapest markets are precisely the two where price is set administratively (Indonesia) or strategically below cost as an ecosystem subsidy to vehicle sales (Vietnam), while the highest prices occur where scarce, licensed capacity meets constrained supply (Singapore).

3.3 Market structures: five archetypes

Table 2 summarizes the five structural archetypes. Vietnam operates a captive vertically integrated model: VinFast (manufacturer) → V-Green (infrastructure, 90% owned by VinFast’s founder) → VinFast vehicles only; independent CPO entry is effectively foreclosed except as V-Green franchisees, who invest in equipment and receive a fixed 750 VND/kWh revenue share guaranteed for at least ten years [8, 9]. Thailand operates an open multi-CPO market in which charging is licensed as an energy business under the Energy Industry Act B.E. 2550 (stations ≥1,000 kVA require a distribution licence; smaller stations notify the ERC), reinforced by EV3.0/EV3.5 demand subsidies and BOI supply-side incentives; new Department of Energy Business technical regulations effective April 2026 raise certification requirements, including mandatory emergency disconnection switches [20–22]. Indonesia operates a utility-anchored partnership model: PLN anchors deployment and retail, private partners join through the Partnership SPKLU scheme (published revenue split: 25% landowner / 73% charger provider / 2% PLN application services) and are exempted from holding their own IUPTL licences [19]. Singapore is a licensed-tender market — operators must hold an LTA licence with uptime, insurance, and data-sharing obligations — and Malaysia is GLC-led, with Petronas’ Gentari and TNB deploying alongside private CPOs who face equipment import duties and must surrender compact substations to TNB even when privately financed [12–15]. The Philippines’ EVIDA statute mandates 5% EV shares in government and corporate fleets, requires DOE accreditation for every commercial charging site, and obliges fuel stations to install chargers [16].

3.4 Infrastructure deployment: installed base versus targets

Figure 3 contrasts installed public charging with national 2030 targets. Indonesia shows the region’s largest absolute gap: 4,655 PLN-network SPKLU units at end-2025 (up 44% from 3,223 in 2024; 633 ultra-fast, 482 fast, 2,681 medium, 859 standard, across 3,007 locations) against a 31,859-unit BKPM target [4, 6, 18]. Singapore has installed 30,500 points (March 2026) toward its 60,000-point target, with every HDB town already EV-ready [12]. Thailand reports roughly 11,500 public points against a 12,000 DC-point 2030 target, while Malaysia’s 5,839 units (March 2026) trail a 10,000-unit target that has been publicly delayed [10, 14, 15]. Vietnam is excluded from the chart because V-Green’s reported >150,000 “ports” (63 provinces, targeting 500,000 by 2028, including two-wheeler outlets and partly planned capacity) are not unit-comparable [29].

3.5 CPO business economics

Hardware capital costs are broadly uniform across the region because equipment is globally traded: AC Level-2 units install at US$3,500–15,000 per port; 50 kW DC hardware costs US$20,000–50,000; 120–180 kW units US$65,000–90,000; and 350 kW-class ultra-fast units US$100,000–175,000, with ultra-fast hardware prices having fallen roughly 20% between 2022 and 2024 [32]. Grid-connection costs can exceed 40% of total investment where a new transformer or substation is required. Recurring operating costs include network fees (US$15–50/charger/month), payment processing (2.5–4.5% plus per-transaction fees), software and connectivity (US$25–60/charger/month combined), and preventive maintenance (US$200–500/charger/year) [32].

What differs across countries is the revenue side. In Indonesia, BKPM cites Rp300–500 million (≈US$18,000–31,000) investment per SPKLU point [18], and an Indonesian feasibility study of a PLN service unit in Makassar found fast charging financially viable (NPV Rp108 million; IRR 45%) while ultra-fast charging failed to reach payback within five years — identifying utilization, not hardware cost, as the binding constraint [30]. Indonesia’s Partnership SPKLU scheme lowers entry barriers (partners need no IUPTL; minimum 6×7 m site; four cooperation models including investor-own–investor-operate) but the capped per-session service fee bounds the revenue ceiling [19]. In Vietnam, the V-Green franchise transfers utilization risk to the franchisor via a fixed 750 VND/kWh fee guaranteed ≥10 years, backed by a 10-trillion-VND (≈US$385 million) two-year investment commitment — an attractive yield instrument, but one that caps upside and serves VinFast vehicles only [8, 9, 29].

4. Discussion

4.1 Market leadership is segment-specific

No single country “leads ASEAN” once the question is disaggregated by investment segment. Thailand leads vehicle manufacturing: the Board of Investment reports over US$4.1 billion (≈137 billion baht) in pledges across 198 EV supply-chain projects, including US$1.18 billion in 18 BEV projects establishing domestic production capacity above 370,000 units per year [20]. Indonesia leads battery and upstream integration, mining roughly 2.6 of the world’s 3.9 million tonnes of nickel in 2025 (≈67%) [25] and hosting the near-US$6 billion CATL–IBC–Antam Indonesia Battery Integration Project (first-phase 6.9 GWh, groundbreaking July 2025) alongside the operational 10 GWh Hyundai–LGES cell plant — although the April 2025 cancellation of the LG-led US$7.7 billion “Grand Package” increased dependence on Chinese partners [24, 26]. Vietnam leads adoption velocity and build-out speed through its captive model, and Singapore leads per-station profitability through the region’s highest tariffs and utilization. For independent CPO investment specifically, Thailand and Malaysia are the most open and therefore most attractive markets; Indonesia offers scale within PLN’s framework; Vietnam is effectively closed.

Figure 4 positions the six markets on two axes — CPO market openness (authors’ qualitative coding of the Section 3.3 evidence) and BEV penetration — with bubble size proportional to installed public charging. The striking feature is the empty upper-right quadrant: no ASEAN market yet combines full openness with high adoption. Vietnam bought speed with captivity; Singapore bought quality with licensing; Thailand and Malaysia are open but must still grow demand; Indonesia sits deliberately mid-spectrum, trading private-margin freedom for regulated affordability.

[gambar: 4af4f19b0421f0710b42962f93196814e55d543d.png]

Figure 4. CPO market openness versus BEV adoption, H1 2026. Openness scores are the authors’ qualitative assessment; bubble sizes indicate installed public chargers (Vietnam nominal). Sources: [1] and Section 3 evidence.

Market-size projections should be read with caution: Mordor Intelligence estimates the ASEAN EV market at US$5.99 billion in 2026 growing to US$23.58 billion by 2031 (CAGR 31.55%, with DC fast charging at 32.85%) [27], while MarkWide Research estimates US$18.7 billion in 2026 reaching US$135.36 billion by 2035 (CAGR 24.60%) [28]. The three-fold divergence for the same base year reflects differing scope definitions; both are vendor estimates.

4.2 Indonesia’s position: structural strength, unit-economic fragility

Indonesia’s 2025 performance was unambiguous on the demand side: BEV sales more than doubled to 106,644 units [23], the public SPKLU network grew 44%, and PLN home-charging subscriptions more than doubled to 70,250 customers, stimulated by a 30% night-tariff discount [4] (Figure 5). Ember places Indonesia’s 2025 BEV share at ≈15%, surpassing the United States for the first time [2].

[gambar: 19a1c319f86004172a504cd299a1b3a53ac59f74.png]

Figure 5. Indonesia’s 2024→2025 growth across public charging, home charging, and BEV sales. 2024 BEV sales shown at ≈52,500 units (2025 reported as “more than double” 2024). Sources: [4, 23].

Table 3 synthesizes Indonesia’s position. The core tension is that the same regulatory choices that make charging affordable and deployment coordinated — regulated energy tariffs, capped session fees, PLN anchoring — also compress the margins that would draw independent capital to low-utilization locations. The Makassar feasibility evidence [30] implies that under current caps, ultra-fast stations outside high-traffic Java corridors are not privately bankable; deployment there will remain PLN-led or subsidy-dependent. This creates a direct efficiency–equity trade-off: building where utilization is high maximizes returns but concentrates access in Jabodetabek and Java, while building where access is lowest requires accepting sub-commercial returns — the central spatial-equity problem for SPKLU policy.

5. Policy and Investment Implications

For investors, the segment-specific reading yields four operational rules:

Independent CPO entry: prioritize Thailand and Malaysia (market pricing, open licensing); in Indonesia, enter via the PLN Partnership scheme (investor-own–investor-operate) in high-utilization Java corridors; avoid standalone ultra-fast stations outside Java absent subsidy.

Vietnam: treat V-Green franchising as a fixed-income-like instrument (750 VND/kWh, ≥10-year guarantee) rather than a growth equity play; do not attempt independent network build-out.

Manufacturing and upstream: vehicle assembly and export — Thailand (BOI/EEC); battery value chain — Indonesia (CATL ecosystem, IBC joint ventures).

Re-rating triggers to monitor: relaxation of Indonesia’s session-fee caps or utilization rising above ≈8–10% outside Java; realization of Malaysia’s delayed 10,000-charger target; resolution of Vietnam’s EV electricity-tariff debate; implementation of Thailand’s April 2026 DOEB technical rules (which raise certification bars and favour internationally documented hardware in tenders).

For Indonesian policymakers, three options follow directly from the evidence. First, utilization-linked incentives or cross-subsidy mechanisms for ex-Java locations would reconcile the efficiency–equity trade-off without abandoning tariff protection for consumers. Second, differentiating the service-fee cap by location class (or converting it to a per-kWh margin with a consumer-price ceiling) would restore private bankability at the margin while preserving affordability. Third, accelerating interoperability — CCS2 hardware standards with OCPP-based roaming across PLN and partner networks — would raise effective utilization of the existing asset base before new capital is deployed.

6. Conclusion

ASEAN’s EV boom is real but structurally heterogeneous: five distinct market architectures produce a five-fold spread in charging prices and sharply different investment propositions. Leadership is segment-specific — Thailand in vehicles, Indonesia in batteries, Vietnam in adoption speed, Singapore in per-station economics — and no market yet combines openness with high adoption. Indonesia enters 2026 with the region’s strongest upstream position and largest deployment pipeline, but its regulated, utility-anchored charging model trades private margin for affordability, leaving spatial equity of access dependent on policy design rather than market forces. The utilization-linked and location-differentiated instruments outlined above offer a path to close that gap without sacrificing the consumer protection that has underpinned Indonesia’s rapid adoption.

Limitations

H1 2026 penetration figures derive from a single research house (Maybank via TNGlobal) and should be treated as estimates pending official statistics.

Charger counts are definitionally incompatible across countries (units vs points vs ports); cross-country density comparisons are deliberately avoided.

Hardware CAPEX benchmarks are largely global rather than ASEAN-specific; local taxes (e.g., Malaysian SST ≥10%) and archipelagic logistics shift landed costs.

Market-size projections conflict three-fold between vendors for the same base year; neither figure is official.

Thailand’s April 2026 technical rules are issued by DOEB while energy licensing sits with the ERC; some secondary sources conflate the two regulators.

Brunei, Cambodia, Laos, and Myanmar are excluded for lack of reliable data.

papers.abstract: The ten ASEAN economies are frequently analysed as a single electric vehicle (EV) market, yet their charging-infrastructure businesses operate under structurally incompatible rules. This paper compares EV adoption, retail charging tariffs, charge-point-operator (CPO) economics, and market/regulatory structures across the six major ASEAN markets — Indonesia, Thailand, Vietnam, Malaysia, Singapore, and the Philippines — using 2025–2026 data drawn from regulators, utilities, operator rate cards, and reputable secondary research. We document a five-fold spread in retail DC fast-charging prices (from ≈US$0.15/kWh in Vietnam’s captive V-Green network and Indonesia’s regulated SPKLU tariff to ≈US$0.70/kWh in Singapore) and classify national market structures into five archetypes: captive vertical integration (Vietnam), open multi-CPO competition (Thailand), utility-anchored partnership (Indonesia), licensed-tender regulation (Singapore), and government-linked-company-led deployment (Malaysia), with a mandate-driven early market in the Philippines. No leadership verdict holds across all investment segments: Thailand leads vehicle manufacturing, Indonesia leads battery/upstream integration, Vietnam leads volume adoption and build-out speed, and Singapore leads per-station profitability. Indonesia holds the region’s largest deployment pipeline (4,655 public SPKLU units in 2025 against a 31,859-unit 2030 target) and doubled BEV sales, home-charging subscriptions, and public-charger growth in a single year, but capped per-session service fees, low utilization outside Java, and an archipelagic geography compress private CPO unit economics. We conclude with segment-specific investment guidance and policy options — including utilization-linked incentives and cross-subsidy mechanisms — that would reconcile Indonesia’s efficiency–spatial-equity trade-off in charger deployment. Keywords: electric vehicles; charging infrastructure; SPKLU; charge point operator; ASEAN; tariff regulation; market structure; Indonesia

Capacity Maps As An Equity Instrument: Publishing Charging Demand And Network Headroom As Open Data In A Vertically Integrated Dso

Qashtalani HARAMAINI Monash University Indonesia / PT PLN (Persero) UID Jawa Barat – Indonesia qashtalani.haramaini@monash.edu · Alyas WIDITA Monash University Indonesia – Indonesia alyas.widita@monash.edu · Liz TAYLOR Monash University, MADA – Australia liz.taylor@monash.edu

Abstract

Distribution system operators (DSOs) increasingly publish hosting-capacity maps to steer connection applicants towards grid nodes with spare capacity. This paper argues that, in a fast-growing network with low electric-vehicle (EV) penetration, such a map is not neutral information but an allocation instrument: what the DSO chooses to publish determines where public charging is built and who is served. West Java, Indonesia, provides a rare test case because PT PLN is simultaneously the DSO and the dominant charge-point operator (CPO) and therefore holds both surfaces that are institutionally separated in Europe: transformer-level load and session-level charging demand. Fusing 53,797 distribution-transformer load surveys with primary-substation linkage, 101,020 charging sessions from 636 public chargers, and 3,687 geocoded registered EV customers on a 5 km grid, we show that (i) the existing charger roll-out tracks grid density rather than spare capacity; (ii) high-demand/low-headroom cells hold 12.8 % of EV owners but only 7.2 % of chargers; (iii) a headroom-only siting rule strands 30 % of a 50-site portfolio in low-demand cells and reaches 12 % fewer owners than a demand-within-headroom rule; (iv) transformer-level and substation-level headroom disagree in 51 % of served cells; and (v) the DSO’s load register is not publication-ready without cleaning, growth correction and aggregation. We propose a minimum standard for publishable two-surface capacity maps and argue that, where the DSO is also the CPO, publication is the functional substitute for unbundling.

1. INTRODUCTION

Grid connection has become the binding constraint on public charging deployment in many jurisdictions [1,3]. In response, European regulation now requires system operators to publish available hosting capacity [1], and DSO associations treat capacity maps as a building block of a customer-oriented grid [2]. The maps are framed as transparency: they inform developers and shorten connection lead times.

This paper starts from a different premise. A capacity map is a ranking of locations, and any ranking that drives investment is also a distribution of benefits. If the only published layer is network headroom, capital flows to where the grid is strong. In mature networks this is largely where load already is; in fast-growing, low-penetration networks it is where the last generation of investment went — typically urban cores and industrial corridors — which is also where charging demand is already served. A headroom-only map therefore tends to densify rather than to fill gaps. This is an energy-justice problem in the sense of Sovacool and Dworkin [6]: a distributive outcome produced by a procedural choice about what to disclose.

Testing this claim empirically requires two surfaces that are rarely held by one organisation: network headroom (a DSO asset) and charging demand (a CPO asset). West Java offers both. PT PLN (Persero) is the vertically integrated utility; its distribution unit UID Jawa Barat operates the 20 kV and low-voltage network for 18.1 million customers, and PLN also operates most of the province’s public charging stations (SPKLU). The authors had access to the transformer load register, the charging transaction log and the EV customer register. To our knowledge this is the first study to overlay all three at province scale.

The contributions are: (1) an empirical test of whether the existing roll-out responds to spare capacity; (2) a demand × headroom classification that isolates the locational equity gap; (3) a counterfactual comparison of three siting rules a DSO could implement through what it publishes; (4) evidence that single-level headroom misclassifies half of the served cells; and (5) a data-readiness audit that translates into a minimum disclosure standard.

2. BACKGROUND AND RESEARCH GAP

2.1 Hosting-capacity maps in Europe

Hosting capacity is the amount of load or generation that can be connected without violating operational limits [8]. Its calculation is sensitive to method: Lennerhag et al. showed at CIRED 2017 that five methods yield widely different values and that measurement-based approaches raise usable capacity without added risk [4]. Since the 2024 electricity market reform, EU system operators must publish available capacity and the criteria used [1]; ENTSO-E and the EU DSO Entity were tasked with harmonised definitions and a pan-European overview. E.DSO’s survey of its members concludes that the priority is not full harmonisation but clearer definitions, stronger links to connection processes and a balanced approach to transparency [2]. ICCT’s 2025 inventory finds public grid-capacity maps for charging in only part of the EU, with uneven voltage coverage [3]. None of these documents treats the map as a distributive instrument.

2.2 Charging-access equity

A separate literature documents that public charger access is unequally distributed across income and ethnicity [5] and clusters with commercial land use [9]. These studies treat the grid as exogenous. Work on EV hosting capacity [10,11] treats demand as exogenous. The two literatures meet only in optimisation models that co-locate chargers with grid capacity [12], which assume a single planner holding both datasets — precisely the situation in a vertically integrated utility.

2.3 Indonesia

Presidential Regulation 55/2019 launched Indonesia’s battery-EV programme; ministerial rules set a 50 kW threshold for public fast charging and tariff structures for SPKLU [7]. PLN reports 3 % electricity sales growth and 5.9 % connected-capacity growth in West Java in 2025 [13]. EV penetration remains below 1 % of the vehicle stock, so the charging network is being built ahead of demand — the regime in which the published layer matters most.

3. CASE AND DATA

Three datasets were assembled (Table 1). The transformer register is a field-survey database: two spot readings (day and night) of phase currents per distribution transformer, with rated kVA, feeder, primary substation (GI) and coordinates from two sources (survey and asset register). The charging log contains every session at PLN’s public chargers in March 2026 with energy, duration and revenue. The EV customer register lists households that applied for the home-charging tariff, geocoded at the service point; it is used as a latent-demand proxy that is independent of where public chargers were built.

4. METHOD

4.1 Two-level headroom

For each transformer i with rated capacity Si and measured loading λi (share of nominal current, maximum of day and night), headroom at the 80 % planning limit is Hi = max(0, Si·(0.8 − λi)). Records failing basic plausibility (invalid coordinates, S outside 5–3,000 kVA, λ outside 0–200 %) were dropped, leaving 41,129. Primary-substation headroom is computed identically from GI transformer MVA and loading (182 GI transformers, 9,790 MVA). Each 5 km cell receives the sum of transformer headroom and the mean headroom of the GI(s) supplying it.

4.2 Growth correction

Surveys are dated; the median reading is 2.3 years old and the oldest 6.2 years. Loading was compounded to March 2026 as λ(2026) = λ(t)·(1+g)2026.2−t. The base case uses g = 3.0 %/yr, the DSO’s reported 2025 sales growth [13]; sensitivities use 5.9 %/yr (connected-capacity growth) and 9.7 %/yr (the median cross-sectional slope of loading on survey date within UP3 units, which is an upper bound because 2020 readings were COVID-depressed).

4.3 Grid, classification and siting rules

All layers were aggregated to a 0.045° (≈5 km) grid of 1,292 cells; 235 contain registered EV owners and 174 contain a public charger. Cells with EV owners were classified by median demand (EV owners) × median headroom. Three siting rules were then applied to the 129 unserved cells with EV owners, each selecting 50 cells: headroom-only (rank by H), demand-only (rank by EV owners), and demand-within-headroom (rank by EV owners subject to H ≥ 240 kVA, i.e. one 4×60 kW site). Outcomes: owners newly reached, sites in below-median-demand cells (stranded capital), sites below the feasibility threshold, regencies covered, and the between-regency Gini of the share of EV owners living in a cell with a charger.

5. RESULTS

5.1 The roll-out follows grid density, not spare capacity

Across served cells, charging energy correlates with absolute headroom (Spearman ρ = 0.42, p < 10−8) but not with headroom as a share of installed capacity (ρ = −0.06, p = 0.43). Absolute headroom scales with the number of transformers, i.e. with urbanisation; relative headroom measures spare capacity. Chargers were therefore placed where the grid is dense, blind to whether it is loaded. Fig. 1 shows the resulting pattern: 42 % of the province’s growth-adjusted headroom lies in cells with no public charger, and a quarter of registered EV owners live in those cells.

5.2 The equity gap is locational

Fig. 2 classifies the 235 cells with EV owners. The high-demand/high-headroom quadrant holds 84.9 % of owners and 79.9 % of chargers — the roll-out is broadly rational. The gap is the high-demand/low-headroom quadrant: 12.8 % of owners, 7.2 % of chargers, and 37 cells with 270 owners and no charger at all. These are the cells a headroom-only map would rank last and a demand-only map would rank first without warning the developer of the connection cost.

5.3 The published layer changes the portfolio

Table 2 and Fig. 3 compare the three siting rules. The headroom-only rule reaches 694 of the 901 owners in unserved cells and places 15 of 50 sites in cells with below-median demand. The demand-only rule reaches 807 owners but places 2 sites below the feasibility threshold and is the most geographically concentrated (15 regencies). The demand-within-headroom rule strands no site, reaches 789 owners (+12 % on headroom-only), spreads over 17 regencies and lowers the between-regency coverage Gini from 0.69 today to 0.60. The result is stable across growth scenarios (789, 789 and 788 owners reached at 3.0, 5.9 and 9.7 %/yr).

5.4 One level is not enough

Of the 174 served cells, 42 have tight transformer headroom but ample GI headroom and 46 the reverse — 51 % discordant. A map showing only the low-voltage level would tell a developer to avoid cells where a new dedicated transformer on a lightly loaded feeder is cheap; a map showing only the substation level would hide that the last 400 m of network is saturated. Both levels must be published, and the full paper adds the intermediate feeder level (2,574 feeders, Table 1).

5.5 Ageing and data readiness

Growth correction at 3.0 %/yr moves 7,088 transformers (17 % of usable records) past the 80 % limit and reduces province-wide headroom from 2,624 to 2,392 MVA at transformer level and from 2,377 to 1,912 MVA at GI level; at 9.7 %/yr the reductions are 26 % and 52 % (Fig. 4, right). The underlying register is not publication-ready (Fig. 4, left): 44 % of records are not linked to a primary substation, 38 % have survey coordinates more than 1 km from the asset register, 23 % have no load reading and 22 % no rated capacity. The register also contains field-staff names and customer-identifying transformer labels that must be removed before disclosure.

6. DISCUSSION

6.1 A minimum standard for publishable capacity maps

The results translate into five requirements. (1) Two levels at least — transformer and primary substation — with the feeder level where available. (2) Growth correction with a stated rate and survey date, since a static snapshot overstates headroom within two years. (3) A demand layer alongside headroom: registered EV customers, predicted energy, or both. (4) Spatial aggregation (here 5 km cells; 2 km hexagons in the companion siting tool) to protect customer and staff privacy and critical-infrastructure detail, consistent with E.DSO’s call for balanced transparency [2]. (5) Versioning and a published data-quality score, so that a map that misdirects private capital can be corrected rather than trusted.

6.2 Publication as a substitute for unbundling

EU DSOs are generally barred from owning charging points precisely because of the information advantage documented here. Indonesia has chosen the opposite structure. In that structure the incumbent can, in principle, site its own chargers on its own knowledge of headroom and demand while third-party CPOs cannot. Publishing the two-surface map removes that asymmetry without changing ownership: it is the functional substitute for unbundling, and it steers all capital — public and private — towards gap-filling rather than densification.

6.3 Limitations

Headroom is derived from two spot readings per transformer, not continuous metering; it is a planning proxy, not a hosting-capacity calculation in the sense of [4,8]. At 5 km resolution aggregate headroom is rarely binding (only 2 of 50 demand-only sites fall below 240 kVA); the binding constraint is locational, at the transformer and feeder, which the full analysis will resolve. Registered EV customers are a proxy for latent demand and under-represent households without a home charger. The growth rate is province-wide; unit-level rates would sharpen the correction. Finally, the counterfactual assumes 50 equal sites; a capacity-weighted portfolio may change the magnitudes but not the ordering.

7. CONCLUSIONS

In a vertically integrated DSO building charging ahead of demand, the capacity map is a planning decision disguised as a data product. Publishing headroom alone reproduces the geography of the existing grid; publishing headroom and demand together, at two network levels, with growth correction and a data-quality score, redirects a fixed budget towards the cells where EV owners are already waiting. The West Java evidence — 12 % more owners reached, no stranded sites, a broader regional spread and a lower coverage Gini for the same 50 sites — is modest in magnitude but unambiguous in direction, and it is obtainable from data every DSO already holds.

From Energy Forecast to Network Load: A Demand Modelling Methodology for EV Charging in Distribution Network Development Planning

Qashtalani HARAMAINI — Monash University, Indonesia / PT PLN (Persero) — qashtalani.haramaini@pln.co.id

Paper prepared for CIRED 2027, Session 5 — Planning of Power Distribution Systems (Demand and Generation Forecast)

Abstract

Ex-ante models can now predict how much energy a public electric-vehicle charging site will sell before it is built. A distribution network development plan (DNDP), however, is not denominated in kilowatt-hours per month; it is denominated in kilowatts at a named transformer, at the hour the network peaks. This paper supplies the missing translation layer and demonstrates it on a full-scale utility dataset: 101,020 revenue-grade charging sessions from 328 public stations, joined to the measured loading of 41,128 distribution transformers across West Java, Indonesia.

Three results follow. First, public fast charging is not an off-peak load: reconstructed at 15-minute resolution, the aggregate charging curve retains 88–91% of its daily maximum throughout the 18:00–22:00 evening peak window, and 20.4% of monthly energy is delivered in those four hours against 16.7% under a flat profile. Second, the relationship between forecast energy and design peak is strongly sub-linear, P = 0.133·E^0.695 (R² = 0.810), so the nameplate-times-coincidence rule that dominates connection studies over-estimates 74% of sites and carries 1.7 times the error of an energy-based rule. Third, inverting the transfer function prices network headroom in the same unit as the demand forecast: the 41,128 transformers can host 452 GWh/month of charging in aggregate, roughly twenty times the 2030 provincial requirement, yet under a demand-led rollout 49% of the transformers that host charging today would exceed 100% loading, and the 13% of 2 km cells in deficit contain 46% of the forecast energy. Reallocating half of the increment under the statutory coverage obligation removes the violation entirely. Charging demand in this network is therefore not a capacity problem but an allocation problem, and the coverage mandate is a network-relief instrument rather than a network cost.

1. INTRODUCTION

Electromobility has become the fastest-moving line in most distribution demand forecasts, and Indonesia is a useful extreme case because the rollout is mandated rather than merely projected. Ministerial Decree Kepmen ESDM 24.K/TL.01/MEM.L/2025 raises the national public charging target from 5,810 units in 2025 to 62,918 units by 2030 and attaches a spatial equity obligation to the trajectory: for every five units built in the Jakarta metropolitan area, and for every twelve built elsewhere outside provincial capitals, one must be sited in a non-dense area. For the distribution system operator this is a planning input with an unusual property — the quantity of stations is fixed by statute, while their location, rating and connection point are not.

Two literatures address parts of the resulting problem and neither closes it. Siting studies rank candidate locations by weighted suitability layers or by flow capture, producing an ordinal score [1], [2], [3]. Demand-forecasting studies predict occupancy or load at stations that already exist, over horizons of hours to days [4], [5]. A recent companion study to this paper closes one gap by predicting, ex ante, the monthly energy a site will sell before it is built, calibrated against billed transactions [6]. What none of them produces is the object a DNDP consumes: a kilowatt value, attached to a specific medium- or low-voltage asset, at the hour that asset peaks.

The translation is not arithmetic. Between an energy forecast and a feeder loading forecast sit three quantities that must be measured rather than assumed: the shape of the charging load through the day, and specifically how much of it survives into the network peak window; the ratio between monthly energy and design peak at a single site, which is not constant across site sizes; and the diversity that accrues when several sites share a feeder or a supply substation. Planning practice fills these gaps with rules of thumb — nameplate rating multiplied by an assumed coincidence factor, an assumed load factor, an assumed off-peak profile. Each of these can be tested against measurement, and this paper tests all three.

The contributions are:

A measured charging load profile at network scale, reconstructed from 101,020 sessions, showing that public charging in this network coincides almost fully with the evening distribution peak rather than avoiding it.

An energy-to-peak transfer function estimated on 296 stations, with a sub-linear exponent that is inconsistent with constant-load-factor scaling, and a quantified comparison against the nameplate rule it is intended to replace.

An empirical coincidence curve for aggregations of charging sites, usable directly at feeder and supply-substation level.

Network headroom expressed in kilowatt-hours per month, obtained by inverting the transfer function over the measured loading of 41,128 distribution transformers. This puts capacity and demand in a common currency and makes the two directly comparable at any spatial resolution.

A spatial scenario test to 2030 under the statutory trajectory, comparing a demand-led allocation with the coverage-obligated allocation, and reporting the network consequence of each.

Everything reported here is derived from data a vertically integrated utility already holds — a charge-point management system and a distribution transformer load register — with no vehicle trajectory data, no smart-meter feed and no proprietary mobility product.

2. STUDY AREA AND DATA

The study area is the service territory of PLN UID Jawa Barat, the densest electric-vehicle corridor in Indonesia, covering 25 regencies and cities. Three registers are used (Table 1).

The transaction layer comprises 101,020 charging sessions recorded at 330 public stations over 1–31 March 2026 by the charge-point management system, at revenue-grade metering accuracy — the same measurement chain used for billing. Aggregated to the station, the network delivered 2,258 MWh in the window at 22.37 kWh per session and a mean session duration of 53.8 minutes. Two stations lack usable coordinates and are excluded, leaving 328; stations with no transactions are retained at zero.

The network layer is the distribution transformer register for the same territory: 53,797 records, of which 41,128 carry a valid coordinate, a capacity between 5 and 3,000 kVA and a plausible loading measurement. Loading is recorded as the three-phase average current measured twice, once in the daytime off-peak window (LWBP, nominally 10:00–14:00) and once in the evening peak window (WBP, nominally 18:00–22:00), expressed against the transformer’s nominal current. Median measured loading is 28.3% by day and 44.2% at night; 11.8% of transformers exceed 80% at night and 3.0% exceed 100%. Installed distribution capacity totals 7,802 MVA. Each record also carries its feeder and supply substation identity, allowing results to be aggregated upward.

The station register supplies the connector configuration and nameplate rating of each charging site, used as the comparator for the transfer function.

3. METHOD

3.1 Reconstructing the charging load

Each session carries a start timestamp, a duration and a delivered energy. Session power is taken as delivered energy over duration, capped at the charger’s nameplate rating to suppress metering and idle-time artefacts, and distributed over 15-minute bins from the start time with the final bin partially filled so that energy is conserved. This produces a 328 × 2,976 station–time matrix of average power for the month. The mean reconstructed session power is 34.5 kW and the median 30.2 kW, consistent with a network dominated by 60–200 kW direct-current equipment.

Two aggregation windows are then defined to match the measurement convention of the transformer register: the daytime window (10:00–14:00) and the evening window (18:00–22:00). For each station i we extract the absolute monthly maximum Pᵢ^own, the maximum within the evening window Pᵢ^WBP, and the mean within the evening window.

3.2 The energy-to-peak transfer function

A DNDP needs to convert a forecast quantity of energy into a design load. We estimate the relation directly in logarithms,

log Pᵢ = log a + b log Eᵢ + εᵢ (1)

where Eᵢ is monthly energy in kWh and Pᵢ is the relevant peak in kW, fitted on the 296 stations with more than 100 kWh in the month. Two variants are reported: P^own, the value a dedicated service transformer must carry, and P^WBP, the value that must be added to the host transformer’s measured evening loading. A third variant using the mean of the evening window gives the expected contribution appropriate for aggregation over many sites.

The competing convention is the nameplate rule, P = CF · Σ rated kW, which is compared on the same data by regressing log P^WBP on log nameplate, and by evaluating the fixed rule CF = 0.6 used in current connection practice.

3.3 Coincidence across sites

The coincidence factor of an aggregation of n sites is estimated empirically rather than assumed. For each n in a geometric ladder, 200 random subsets of stations are drawn, the group maximum within the evening window is divided by the sum of the members’ individual evening maxima, and the mean and standard deviation are recorded. The result is a diversity curve directly usable at feeder level (small n) and supply-substation level (large n).

3.4 Network headroom priced in kilowatt-hours

The transfer function is monotone and therefore invertible. For a transformer with capacity S and measured evening loading λ, the spare capacity to an 80% planning limit is

ΔS = max(0.8·S − λ·S, 0) (2)

and the quantity of monthly charging energy that spare capacity can host is

E^host = (ΔS / a)^(1/b) (3)

with a, b from the P^WBP fit. Equation (3) is the pivot of the paper. It converts every transformer in the register into an energy quantity denominated exactly like the output of the ex-ante demand model, so that supply and demand can be differenced at any spatial unit — transformer, 2 km cell, feeder, supply substation, or service area — without further conversion. The 80% limit is a conservative planning convention rather than a thermal limit; it can be relaxed with a loading-guide assessment where cyclic ratings apply.

3.5 Spatial allocation of the statutory trajectory

The 2030 forecast is anchored on the statutory unit trajectory, a factor of 10.83 between the 2025 and 2030 targets, applied to observed provincial charging energy to give 24.4 GWh/month. Two allocations of the same total are compared.

Demand-led. The increment is distributed in proportion to observed station energy, i.e. growth occurs where charging already happens. This is the allocation that an unconstrained commercial rollout, or a siting model optimised on predicted sales alone, would produce.

Coverage-led. Half the increment is distributed as above and half is spread over transformers in areas with no charging today, weighted by their available headroom. This approximates the spatial effect of the equity clause of the decree.

For each allocation, site energy is converted to evening-window load by (1), added to the host transformer’s measured evening loading, and the resulting loading distribution is reported. Each station is assigned to its nearest transformer as a proxy for the connection point; the median station-to-transformer distance is 121 m and the 90th percentile 828 m, so the proxy is tight in the urban core and looser along corridors.

4. RESULTS

4.1 Public charging is not an off-peak load

Figure 1 (left) gives the aggregate charging curve averaged over the 31 days. It peaks at 15:00, but the more consequential feature is its flatness: the curve holds 87.5–91.1% of its daily maximum right through the 18:00–22:00 evening window, and 20.4% of monthly energy is delivered in those four hours, against 16.7% under a flat profile. At station level the same conclusion holds individually: the median station’s maximum inside the evening window is 0.93 of its absolute monthly maximum (interquartile range 0.79–1.00). The absolute network maximum of 8.26 MW occurred at 17:15 on 22 March.

This matters because the distribution network in this territory is evening-peaking. Figure 1 (right) contrasts the measured daytime and evening loading of the 41,128 transformers: the daytime distribution is concentrated below 40%, the evening distribution is shifted up by roughly 16 percentage points at the median, and the population above the 80% planning limit is almost entirely an evening phenomenon. Public charging therefore lands on the constrained window, not the spare one. A planning assumption that public fast charging is a daytime load — common in studies transferred from residential charging, where the coincidence with the evening peak is the classic concern — inverts the actual risk in this network: here the daytime component is real, but it does not reduce the evening contribution.

The curve retains 88-91% of its maximum through the evening window. 4.2 The transfer function, and why nameplate rules mis-size connections

Figure 2 shows the fitted relation between monthly energy and evening-window peak across four orders of magnitude of station size. The design-peak fit is

P^Wbp = 0.133 · E^0.695 (R² = 0.810)

and the own-peak fit P^own = 0.258 · E^0.633 (R² = 0.829). The expected contribution over the evening window is essentially linear in energy, P = 0.0011 · E^1.041 (R² = 0.956), which is the appropriate quantity when many sites are aggregated.

The exponent is the substantive result. It is far below unity, so peak does not scale with energy: a site selling ten times more energy needs only about five times the connection capacity. The mechanism is legible — high-energy sites are busy for more of the day, so their load factor is better. Median load factor rises from about 0.04 in the lowest-selling quartile to 0.14 at highway rest areas, the highest-energy category. A constant-load-factor assumption, which is implicit whenever a planner scales peak linearly with forecast energy, therefore over-sizes large connections and under-sizes small ones simultaneously.

Table 2 compares the candidate rules on the same 296 stations. The nameplate regression explains 70.8% of variance in evening peak with a root-mean-square error of 64.4 kW; the energy transfer function reaches 81.0% at 38.5 kW, a 40% reduction in error. Using both inputs — the equipment the developer proposes and the energy the demand model forecasts — gives P^WBP = 0.126 · N^0.403 · E^0.484 with R² = 0.855 and RMSE 25.8 kW, and is the form we recommend for connection screening, since both inputs are available at application. The fixed rule CF = 0.6 applied to nameplate over-estimates the evening peak at 74% of sites, with a mean absolute error of 43.6 kW — an error large enough, at typical Indonesian distribution transformer sizes, to trigger unnecessary reinforcement at a majority of connection points.

4.3 Diversity is exhausted early

Figure 3 gives the measured coincidence curve. Two sites on a common feeder already coincide at 0.84, five at 0.72, twelve at 0.61, and the curve flattens near 0.45 beyond about fifty sites. The planning default of 0.6 is therefore approximately correct only in a narrow band around a dozen aggregated sites; it is optimistic for the two-to-five-site case that dominates real feeders, and pessimistic at supply-substation scale. The flatness is a direct consequence of the profile result in §4.1 — loads that are individually flat and simultaneously present do not diversify. Charging sites behave, for planning purposes, more like industrial process load than like residential load.

4.4 Headroom, priced in the same unit as demand

Applying (2) and (3) to the register gives 2,902 MVA of evening headroom to the 80% limit, equivalent to 452 GWh/month of hostable charging energy. Set against the 2030 provincial requirement of 24.4 GWh/month, the aggregate ratio is about twenty to one. The distribution, however, is extremely uneven (Table 3): the median transformer can host only 4,675 kWh/month, roughly the output of a single well-used 60 kW unit, while the 125 best-placed transformers could between them host the entire provincial 2030 demand. Sixty-three per cent of all hosting capacity sits in 2 km cells where no charging takes place today.

Figure 4 (right) makes the consequence explicit at 2 km resolution. Of the 222 cells that host charging, 28 — 13% — would see forecast 2030 charging exceed local hosting capacity, but those 28 cells contain 46% of the forecast energy. This is the characteristic signature of a network whose problem is allocation rather than capacity: an aggregate surplus of twenty to one coexisting with binding local deficits that account for nearly half the load.

The same screening applied to today’s network is already informative. Of the 328 existing stations, the evening-window load implied by their measured energy exceeds the headroom of the nearest transformer at 111 sites, 33.8% of the network, and the median station consumes 26.8% of its host transformer’s headroom. Some of these sites are in fact fed by dedicated transformers not identifiable in the register, which is a limitation of the nearest-asset proxy; but the order of magnitude indicates that charging connections in this territory are already a material driver of low-voltage loading rather than a marginal one.

4.5 The 2030 trajectory under two spatial allocations

Figure 5 and Table 4 report the network outcome of the two allocations of the same 24.4 GWh/month.

Under the demand-led allocation, growth concentrates on the 296 transformers that host charging today. Their median evening loading moves from 41.7% to 98.2%; 60% cross the 80% planning limit and 49% cross 100%. In other words, an unconstrained commercial rollout of the statutory number of units would push half of its own host transformers past nameplate at the evening peak, and would do so on assets that are, by construction, in the busiest parts of the network where reinforcement is most expensive and most disruptive.

Under the coverage-led allocation, half the increment is absorbed by 19,740 previously unserved transformers with headroom, at a mean addition of 10.5 kW each. No transformer in that leg crosses the 80% limit. The demand-led half continues to load the existing hosts, but at half the increment the number crossing 100% falls correspondingly.

The policy reading is direct, and it reinforces from the network side a conclusion reached in the companion study on commercial grounds [6], namely that mandated coverage sites are the most productive per site rather than a subsidy to be minimised. Here the same obligation turns out to be a network-relief instrument: it moves load from the transformers least able to accept it onto assets with 2.9 GVA of measured, unused evening headroom. Coverage and capacity are aligned, not opposed.

5. IMPLICATIONS FOR DISTRIBUTION NETWORK DEVELOPMENT PLANS

Four consequences follow for the practice of distribution planning under an electromobility mandate.

Connection screening should be energy-based, not nameplate-based. The combined rule in §4.2 uses only quantities available when a connection is requested and reduces sizing error by 60% against the fixed coincidence rule. Applied across a mandate of tens of thousands of units, the difference between a rule that over-estimates three-quarters of sites and one that does not is a large volume of avoided or deferred reinforcement.

Hosting capacity should be published in the unit the demand forecast uses. Equation (3) allows a DSO to publish, per feeder or per cell, how many kilowatt-hours of monthly charging can be accommodated before reinforcement is triggered. Developers can then self-screen against a public number, and the tender process for mandated sites can be constrained to locations where the network is ready. This is a low-cost intervention: it requires no new measurement, only a transformation of a register the DSO already maintains.

Spatial allocation belongs inside the demand forecast, not after it. The two scenarios differ by no energy at all and by a factor of ten in transformer violations. A DNDP that consumes a provincial energy forecast without a spatial allocation rule cannot see this difference, and will either over-reinforce uniformly or discover the deficits at connection time.

The equity obligation should be planned as a network asset. Because the coverage clause directs sites toward areas with low existing charging density — which are, in this network, the areas with unused evening headroom — compliance and network relief coincide. This should be exploited deliberately: the clause defines a set of eligible locations, and the hosting-capacity map defines which of those locations are cheapest to connect. The intersection is the buildable set.

6. LIMITATIONS

The calibration window is one month, so seasonal variation — particularly the holiday travel peaks that dominate corridor sites — is not resolved, and the transfer function should be re-estimated on a multi-month window before it is used for firm capacity decisions. Transformer loading is a two-point manual measurement rather than a continuous record, so the evening value is a snapshot and the resulting headroom is an estimate with unquantified measurement error. The connection point of each station is proxied by the nearest transformer; sites fed by dedicated transformers or at medium voltage are consequently mis-assigned, which inflates the count of apparently over-loaded hosts in §4.4. The transfer function is estimated on a fleet-to-charger ratio characteristic of an early market; as utilisation rises, load factors will improve and the exponent should be re-estimated, which is itself a testable prediction. Finally, the scenario growth factor is taken from a statutory unit target and assumes constant energy per unit; a demand-side model of fleet growth would replace this with a behavioural projection.

7. CONCLUSION

Ex-ante prediction of charging energy is now feasible from data a distribution utility already owns. This paper supplies the layer that converts such a forecast into a network planning input and demonstrates it on 101,020 metered sessions and 41,128 measured distribution transformers.

Three measured quantities replace three assumptions. Public charging in this network coincides with the evening distribution peak at 0.93 of its own maximum rather than avoiding it. The design peak of a site scales as the 0.70 power of its monthly energy, so nameplate-times-coincidence rules over-estimate three sites in four and carry 1.7 times the error of an energy-based rule. Diversity between charging sites is exhausted by about fifty sites at a coincidence factor of 0.45, well below the planning default over the range that matters at feeder level.

Inverting the transfer function prices the network in the same unit as the forecast. On that basis West Java holds twenty times the hosting capacity its 2030 charging mandate requires, and would still push half of its currently charging-hosting transformers past 100% loading if the mandate were allocated by demand alone. The statutory coverage obligation, allocated instead across transformers with measured spare evening capacity, eliminates the violation. The mandate and the network are not in tension; they are in tension only with a rollout that ignores where the headroom is.
